sources.title: A Note on στεφάνων καθαίρεσις in the Newly Published Papyrus on the Theadelpheia Festival
sources.publisher: Lucia Prauscello (2023); Zeitschrift für Papyrologie und Epigraphik 226; pp. 99–106
sources.period: Alexandrian programme probably from 242 BCE, earlier than the game cohort
sources.geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
sources.summary: Alexandrian festival organization, venues, sponsorship and practical coordination. Read scope: Relevant full-text sections pp.99–100,102,104–105 and conclusion.
sources.limitations: Programme probably belongs to242BCE, an earlier precedent. Crown-handling interpretations remain disputed; no literal event recreation for this cohort. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

sources.title: A Late First Century BC Greek Astronomical Almanac: P.Petrie Mus. astr.
sources.publisher: Gaia Fanelli, Alexander Jones (2019); Zeitschrift für Papyrologie und Epigraphik 212; pp. 199–213
sources.period: Late first century BCE, reconstructed late-Augustan astronomical work
sources.geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
sources.summary: Calculated planetary tables, copying and consultation; probable use as horoscope inputs. Read scope: Introduction pp.199–200 and commentary/reconstruction pp.205–213; no independent collation of fragment readings.
sources.limitations: Provenance unknown. Reconstructed late-Augustan dates fall late in the cohort; appropriate for optional later work, not the sole first accomplishment or proof of Alexandrian employment. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

sources.title: Parapēgmata and poleis: astrometeorological calendars in the Hellenistic city
sources.publisher: Ruben Post (2025); The Journal of Hellenic Studies 145; pp. 1–21; DOI 10.1017/S0075426925100293
sources.period: Hellenistic city calendars, including earlier Egyptian comparative material
sources.geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
sources.summary: Hellenistic calendar compilation and discussion of observation, regional applicability and unreliable forecasts. Read scope: Abstract and relevant full-text sections pp.1–4,6–8.
sources.limitations: Broad Hellenistic evidence; Egyptian P.Hib.27 is earlier and no specific Alexandrian occupation is established. Weather lore is not validated prediction. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

sources.title: Pythagoreanising Aristotle: Eudorus and the systematisation of Platonism
sources.publisher: Mauro Bonazzi (2013); Aristotle, Plato and Pythagoreanism in the First Century BC: New Directions for Philosophy, Cambridge University Press; pp. 160–186; DOI 10.1017/CBO9781139096713.010
sources.period: First-century BCE Alexandrian philosophical interpretation
sources.geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
sources.summary: First-centuryBCE Alexandrian philosophical argument and competing interpretations. Read scope: Author institutional abstract and publisher metadata only.
sources.limitations: Intellectual study, not evidence for universal schooling, ordinary teaching wages or easy access to elite patronage. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

sources.title: Egyptian Warriors: The Machimoi of Herodotus and the Ptolemaic Army
sources.publisher: Christelle Fischer-Bovet (2013); The Classical Quarterly 63(1); pp. 209–236; DOI 10.1017/S000983881200064X
sources.period: Ptolemaic military participation with earlier literary comparisons
sources.geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
sources.summary: Reassessment of Egyptian military participation and simplistic inherited ethnic/status categories. Read scope: Publisher extract and bibliographic metadata only.
sources.limitations: Does not establish unrestricted enlistment, promotion chances or a specific cohort member's military career. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

sources.title: Ptolemaic Berenike: Resources, Logistics, and Daily Life in a Hellenistic Fortress on the Red Sea Coast of Egypt
sources.publisher: Marek A. Woźniak, Steven E. Sidebotham, Marta Osypińska, Alfredo Carannante, Joanna K. Rądkowska (2021); American Journal of Archaeology 125(2); pp. 247–281; DOI 10.3764/aja.125.2.0247
sources.period: Ptolemaic Berenike, a Red Sea port and fortress
sources.geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
sources.summary: Connections between ports, supply, water, military needs and civilian activity. Read scope: Abstract and introduction/methods/geographical sections pp.247–251.
sources.limitations: Berenike is on the Red Sea, not Alexandria. These networks inspire authored voyage-linked stories; a new playable location is not implied. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

sources.title: Strabo, Geography 17.1.6–8: Rhakotis and Alexandria
sources.publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; H. L. Jones, Loeb translation (1932)
sources.period: Augustan-era account describing the earlier settlement and Alexander's foundation
sources.geography: Egyptian Mediterranean coast, Rhakotis and Alexandria
sources.summary: Describes Rhakotis as a settlement preceding Alexandria, the suitability of the harbor and the tradition of Alexander directing the city's foundation.
sources.limitations: Written centuries after the foundation. Its later urban description is not a map of the coast in 350 BCE. The settlement's extent, inhabitants and individual household experiences are not established by this account.

sources.title: Alexandria, Egypt, before Alexander the Great: A multidisciplinary approach yields rich discoveries
sources.publisher: Jean-Daniel Stanley and colleagues, GSA Today 17(8), 2007; doi:10.1130/GSAT01708A.1
sources.period: Pre-Alexandrian activity, with sediment-core evidence extending to about 1000 BCE
sources.geography: Alexandria's East Harbor and adjacent mainland coast
sources.summary: Archaeological, sedimentary and geochemical indicators support human activity on the coast long before Alexander and a pre-existing settlement beneath the later city.
sources.limitations: The exact location, size and organization of Rhakotis remain uncertain. This evidence does not supply a detailed 350 BCE city plan or demographic rates. The paper uses 332 BCE for Alexandria's foundation; the game adopts the conventional 331 BCE year from its separate chronology source.

sources.title: Egypt in the Ptolemaic Period
sources.publisher: Marsha Hill, Department of Egyptian Art, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2016)
sources.period: Egypt before Alexander and the Ptolemaic period, including 343, 332 and 305 BCE
sources.geography: Egypt and the western Nile Delta
sources.summary: Places Persian reconquest in 343 BCE, Alexander's takeover in 332 BCE and Ptolemy's kingship in 305 BCE. It also describes earlier Greek-Egyptian trade through Delta ports and Naukratis.
sources.limitations: An institutional overview rather than a household history. Political dates do not establish every local response, equal access to professions or the game's numerical rewards. Ptolemy governing after Alexander's death must be distinguished from his later adoption of kingship.

sources.title: The Rise of Macedon and the Conquests of Alexander the Great
sources.publisher: Colette Hemingway and Seán Hemingway, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2004)
sources.period: Fourth-century BCE Macedon; Alexander's reign of 336–323 BCE and Asian campaign from 334 BCE
sources.geography: Macedon, Greece, Asia and Egypt
sources.summary: Provides the accession and campaign sequence for Alexander, including his crossing into Asia in 334 BCE and the succession crisis following his death.
sources.limitations: A broad political and art-historical account, not evidence that the fictional player met Alexander. Personal conversations, access to his entourage, recruitment outcomes and civilian consequences are authored situations.

sources.title: Pergamon and the Hellenistic Kingdoms of the Ancient World: chronology
sources.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, exhibition catalogue (2016)
sources.period: Late Classical and Hellenistic chronology, including Alexandria's foundation in 331 BCE
sources.geography: Mediterranean and Hellenistic kingdoms
sources.summary: The catalogue chronology dates the foundation of Alexandria to 331 BCE and places it within Alexander's wider campaigns and the emergence of the successor kingdoms.
sources.limitations: A year-level chronology. The game's precise annual ordering is a calendar convention, not a reconstruction of exact foundation ceremonies, building completion dates or individual participation.

sources.title: Aristotle, section 1: Aristotle's Life
sources.publisher: Christopher Shields, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; substantive revision 2020
sources.period: Aristotle, 384–322 BCE; Macedonian tuition from 343 and the Athenian Lyceum from 335 BCE
sources.geography: Stagira, Athens, Assos, Lesbos, Macedon and Chalcis
sources.summary: Reconstructs Aristotle's movements, the invitation to teach Alexander in 343 BCE and his return to Athens to establish the Lyceum in 335 BCE.
sources.limitations: The duration and substance of Alexander's tuition are uncertain. It provides no basis for placing Aristotle in Alexandria. A player's visit, lesson, dialogue or scholarly recognition is fictional and needs an explicit journey to the appropriate place and a compatible date.

sources.title: Euclid of Alexandria: biography and evidence
sources.publisher: J. J. O'Connor and E. F. Robertson, MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
sources.period: Euclid's approximate activity around 300 BCE under Ptolemy I
sources.geography: Alexandria, Egypt
sources.summary: Discusses Euclid's Alexandrian teaching, the Elements and the sparse later testimony linking him to the first Ptolemy.
sources.limitations: His precise birth, death, birthplace and career chronology are uncertain. Circa 300 BCE is an approximate scholarly setting, not an exact publication or appointment date. Anecdotes and a player's personal encounter must not be represented as verified biographical incidents.

sources.title: Intellectual Pursuits of the Hellenistic Age
sources.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History (2007)
sources.period: Early Hellenistic intellectual patronage and later developments
sources.geography: Athens, Alexandria and other Hellenistic centers
sources.summary: Describes Ptolemaic patronage of scholarship and Alexandria's Library and Mouseion as an early Hellenistic intellectual center, with copying, criticism and learned collaboration.
sources.limitations: It does not establish an exact foundation year or prove that particular careers were available before the institutions developed. The game uses an approximate early-third-century opening for its institution-specific opportunities. Later scholars discussed in the overview require their own chronological guards.

sources.title: Reconstructions: The Pharos of Alexandria
sources.publisher: Alexandria and Mediterranean Research Center, Bibliotheca Alexandrina
sources.period: Pharos erection during 283–279 BCE under Ptolemy II; later monuments have separate dates
sources.geography: Alexandria and its Mediterranean coast
sources.summary: Dates the lighthouse to the reign of Ptolemy II, between 283 and 279 BCE, and explains the use of archaeological and historical evidence in modern reconstructions.
sources.limitations: A reconstruction overview, not a fully recovered original building. A completed lighthouse must not appear at the 350 BCE birth or 331 BCE city foundation. Pharos Island existed earlier; its name alone need not imply the lighthouse. The page's Ptolemy III Serapeum belongs after this cohort's age-100 record.

sources.title: The General Tjahapimu
sources.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Egyptian Art; object 08.205.1
sources.period: Dynasty 30, reign of Nectanebo II, 360–343 BCE
sources.geography: Memphis and the Egyptian royal administration
sources.summary: The statue's inscription names Tjahapimu as a brother and father of kings. The museum discusses his royal family relationships and political and military responsibilities.
sources.limitations: Some details of the genealogy remain uncertain. This object does not attest a royal family at Rhakotis, the player's ancestry, inheritance rights or a particular coastal estate. The game's royal household and its personal experiences are fiction.

sources.title: Egypt in the Late Period (ca. 664–332 B.C.)
sources.publisher: Marsha Hill and James P. Allen, The Metropolitan Museum of Art; revised 2018
sources.period: Late Period Egypt, including Dynasty 30 and Persian reconquest in 343 BCE
sources.geography: Egypt, including Memphis and the Nile Delta
sources.summary: Surveys changing government, Egyptian and foreign military communities, temple patronage and elite participation in religious institutions. It places Nectanebo II and the Persian reconquest within the transition to Alexander's conquest.
sources.limitations: A broad historical account covering several centuries, not a census of Rhakotis in 350 BCE. It does not establish the game's household frequencies, starting cash, ability ranges, care arrangements or fictional family outcomes. Later Ptolemaic institutions must not be assumed at birth.

sources.title: Block Statue of the God's Father Pameniuwedja, son of Nesmin and Nestefnut
sources.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Egyptian Art; object 07.228.25
sources.period: Fourth century BCE, Dynasty 30 to early Ptolemaic Period
sources.geography: Egypt; the object does not establish a Rhakotis household
sources.summary: The inscription names a priest's parents and records his father with the same priestly titles, providing an example of family connections within temple service.
sources.limitations: One priestly family does not establish universal hereditary office or the means of every temple household. The fictional player does not inherit a priesthood, education, occupation or guaranteed patronage from this comparison.

sources.title: Farmers in ancient Egypt
sources.publisher: Digital Egypt for Universities, University College London
sources.period: Comparative discussion across ancient Egyptian periods
sources.geography: Egypt; not a household survey of the fourth-century BCE coast
sources.summary: Discusses evidence and uncertainty concerning farming households, land, property and social status. It cautions against simple conclusions about farmers' circumstances.
sources.limitations: The article does not establish the tenancy terms, wealth, legal status or routines of a particular 350 BCE household. The game's tenant-farming family, financial ranges and choices are authored fiction rather than measured historical distributions.

economy.description: Household accounts use drachmas (dr). Net worth includes cash and the estimated sale value of possessions, less debt. Unpaid unavoidable costs can become debt. Amounts are fixed game values, not reconstructed historical prices or wages. There is no modern-currency conversion or automatic interest. The same simplified accounting unit is used across this lifetime's changes of ruler; it does not imply a fixed exchange rate or uniform historical coinage. A voluntarily accepted moneylender loan has its own balance and deadline. Ordinary household debt keeps automatic repayment; this loan must be paid deliberately. Its upfront charge and optional extension charge are fixed game terms, not measured ancient prices. Collectors pursue only that accepted loan.

assets.title: Tool chest
assets.description: Unlocks hinge, strap and fitting repairs at Tool handling 15. Sell for 30 drachmas.

assets.title: Workshop share
assets.description: Earn 10 drachmas each year you survive. Sell for 120 drachmas.

health.description: Early life keeps the easier health rules. From age 18, serious illness episodes use the full age-specific baseline from a Roman Egyptian female life-table comparison. Illness appears, Health falls and a care choice interrupts time before the condition can become fatal. Current Health, care and household support can change the outcome; dangerous choices retain their stated risks. Exact mortality for the Egyptian coast in this era is unknown. The later Roman comparison is an estimate for the setting, not a measured rate for this character. Disease selection, severity and care effects are authored game rules.

relationships.description: Friends, business partners and romantic relationships are explicit ties with people actually met in this life. Friendship and shared work can coexist with a love interest or spouse. Contact, conflict and neglect affect closeness. Ending one role leaves the others intact. Only the existing close household-care rules affect recovery; friends and business partners create no automatic income or extra health bonus. These arrangements and numeric rewards are fictional gameplay.

knowledge.description: Knowledge needs continued use. From age 12, two full years without a recorded learning gain lead to a loss of 1 point per year. Lessons, research, work and events with positive Knowledge effects refresh practice, including at the stat cap. Ageing also reduces Knowledge by 0.5 per year from 50, 1 from 65 and 1.5 from 80. These are authored game rules, not measured cognitive ageing rates. Skill proficiencies are separate.

routes.description: Learn the entrances, finish an engagement and give a host a reason to invite the ensemble back.

achievements.title: A customer's sculpture
achievements.description: Philista keeps the finished figure. Menon names you as its maker when a visitor asks who carved it.

achievements.title: A distinguished relief
achievements.description: The procession relief passes Menon's inspection. Philista accepts the commission, and younger workers come to examine the cuts.

achievements.title: A remembered argument
achievements.description: Kleio can explain your argument about agreements in her own words. Apollonios keeps the checked outline for another lesson.

achievements.title: A teaching circle
achievements.description: Kleio and Apollonios return with objections to your collected discussions. The revised text becomes the basis of regular meetings.

achievements.title: A completed cargo voyage
achievements.description: Tasos signs for the cargo at the landing. Nikeratos keeps your name beside the completed delivery.

achievements.title: A trusted difficult passage
achievements.description: Crew and cargo reach the quay after a difficult passage. Nikeratos recommends you for a task with greater responsibility.

achievements.title: A recorded service assignment
achievements.description: Dion and Herakleides check the unit's stores against your record and enter your name beside the completed assignment.

achievements.title: A service distinction
achievements.description: Dion and Herakleides record your handling of a difficult unit assignment. Their commendation can support an application for further responsibility.

achievements.title: A fulfilled customer order
achievements.description: Berenike accepts the delivered order. Sarapion is paid, and your copy of the account shows the sum you kept.

achievements.title: A repeat supply agreement
achievements.description: Sarapion and Berenike agree to repeat the arrangement. Your seal identifies the orders placed through the venture.

achievements.title: A corrected seasonal table
achievements.description: Heron checks your arithmetic. Isidora keeps the corrected seasonal table, including the distinction between calculated entries and uncertain expectations.

achievements.title: A credited table collection
achievements.description: Heron and Isidora credit the corrections in your compared tables. Your notes show how each calculation was checked and where uncertainty remains.

achievements.title: A paid musical engagement
achievements.description: Melitta performs beside you at Theon's gathering. The agreed programme is finished, and the household pays for the engagement.

achievements.title: A distinguished repeat invitation
achievements.description: Your signals keep the ensemble together through its programme. Theon credits your organisation and commissions another engagement.

influences.label: Alexander levies the city: people of military age must serve, flee or pay.

event.title: A levy in the king's name
event.text: Officers acting for Alexander are filling garrison and supply posts in Egypt. Your name is on the district list of people fit to serve. The recruiting officer will accept a substitute's fee, and some on the list have already left for relatives in the Delta.

choices.text: Answer the levy and report for service

outcomes.text: You serve a season in a coastal garrison and learn drill under a Macedonian officer. The pay is small and the days are long. When your term ends you return to your household.
Your file leader notices that you keep the others in step and the supply tallies honest. He sends your name to an officer with his report before your term ends.

weightModifiers.reason: You already know basic drill
You can keep a supply tally

outcomes.text: A fall on a supply march leaves you lame. You finish your term in the stores and carry the injury home.

weightModifiers.reason: Good health carries you through the marches

choices.text: Leave for relatives in the Delta until the officers move on

outcomes.text: You spend the season in a relative's village, working for your keep. When you come back the officers have moved on, but your neighbours remember that you were gone.

weightModifiers.reason: Relatives are willing to hide you
You can find passage on a river boat

outcomes.text: Officers are checking the boats at the canal. You are brought back, fined and made to serve a season in the garrison after all.

choices.text: Pay the 60-drachma substitute fee

outcomes.text: The officer takes the fee and enters a hired man in your place. Your household keeps its work, and your name comes off the roll.

influences.label: Alexander founds and builds: new work and building plots open in the city.

event.title: Work on the new city
event.text: Surveyors have marked the streets of Alexander's new city beside Rhakotis. Contractors are hiring for walls, quays and houses, and plots along the new streets are being let to anyone who can pay toward the building.

choices.text: Take paid work on the building sites

outcomes.text: You carry stone, mix mortar and learn how the builders set a line. The pay is steady while the work lasts.
A foreman sees that you can keep count and puts you in charge of a work gang's tallies. You finish the season with better pay and a name the contractors know.

weightModifiers.reason: You can keep a work tally

choices.text: Put 40 drachmas toward a share in a building plot

outcomes.text: The street fills faster than the surveyors expected. Your share is let to newcomers, and the rent comes in before the year is out.

weightModifiers.reason: You can judge the contractor's accounts

outcomes.text: Building stalls when the contractor is called away to the harbour works. You sell the share and recover part of your money.

choices.text: Keep to your own work

outcomes.text: You keep to your existing work and watch the new streets fill from a distance.

influences.label: Aristotle founds the Lyceum: young people study notes from his lectures.

event.title: Notes from the Lyceum
event.text: A reader back from Athens has copied notes from Aristotle's lectures at the Lyceum: what things are made of, why they change and how to argue about them. He offers to go through them with any young person who can keep up.

choices.text: Work through the notes with him

outcomes.text: Week after week you test the questions against things you can see: a seed, a tide, a broken pot. You begin to ask why as readily as what.

weightModifiers.reason: You can already read the notes yourself

outcomes.text: Most of the notes are beyond you this year, but the reader leaves you one question to keep: what makes a thing what it is.

choices.text: Keep to your household work

outcomes.text: You thank the reader and keep to your work. Others in the street borrow the notes.

influences.label: Aristotle tutors the court: royal children learn argument and composure.

event.title: A tutor for the royal household
event.text: Your family has engaged a tutor trained in Aristotle's school, as Philip of Macedon once engaged Aristotle for his son. The lessons cover reading, argument, the conduct of rulers and keeping a clear head when others lose theirs.

choices.text: Attend the lessons and argue back

outcomes.text: The tutor makes you defend every claim and answer calmly when pressed. As an exercise he has you check the household guard's supply lists, then writes to their officer commending your work.

choices.text: Spend the hours riding and hunting instead

outcomes.text: You keep to the stables and the hunting grounds. The tutor teaches your cousins, though some of his questions reach you at meals.

influences.label: Euclid opens a school: children learn letters and figures.

event.title: A school of demonstrations
event.text: A teacher following Euclid's method has opened a school near the harbour. Children draw figures in sand trays and must say why each step follows from the last. The fee is small, and some pupils pay in errands.

choices.text: Go to the lessons

outcomes.text: You learn letters from the written propositions and numbers from the figures. By the end of the year you can prove a small thing and say why it holds.

choices.text: Run errands for the school and listen at the door

outcomes.text: You carry water and messages for the teacher and pick up what you can between errands.

influences.label: Euclid keeps to the Museum: gifted readers may be offered a scholar's post.

event.title: A place among the Museum's scholars
event.text: Scholars working beside Euclid at the Museum need a capable reader to check figures and copy proofs. The post carries a stipend and use of the collected books, but the work is exacting and careless help is soon dismissed.

choices.text: Accept the post and work through the proofs

outcomes.text: You check constructions line by line and copy the corrected proofs. At the end of the season the scholars keep your name among those they recommend for paid work.

weightModifiers.reason: Your reckoning is already strong

outcomes.text: An error in your first copied figure costs you the scholars' trust, and the post goes to another reader. You keep what you learned checking their work.

choices.text: Decline and keep your present work

outcomes.text: You decline the post. The scholars find another reader, and your own work goes on as before.

influences.label: Cleomenes corners the grain: merchants profit while poor households go short.

event.title: Grain held for the export price
event.text: Cleomenes, who manages Egypt's revenues for the king, has bought up the district's grain to sell to famine-struck Greek cities at a high price. Bread in the market now costs twice what it did. Merchants with silver are buying shares in the cargoes; everyone else must pay or go short.

choices.text: Put 40 drachmas into a share of an export cargo

outcomes.text: The cargo sells in a hungry Greek port at the price Cleomenes set. Your share comes back nearly doubled, though your neighbours know where the profit came from.

weightModifiers.reason: You can check the cargo accounts
You already work in the trade

outcomes.text: The ship is held at the harbour while officials argue over the export duty. When the share is finally settled, you recover only part of your money.

choices.text: Pay the high price to keep the household fed

outcomes.text: You pay what the sellers ask. The household eats as before, but your savings are thinner by the end of the season.

choices.text: Eat less until the price falls

outcomes.text: Meals shrink to bread and a little oil. The household gets through the season weaker and short-tempered.
Neighbours pool what they have and share it out. The season is lean, but nobody in the street goes entirely without bread.

weightModifiers.reason: Neighbours share with people they trust

influences.label: Cleomenes fills the granaries: rations reach struggling households in a lean season.

event.title: The granaries open
event.text: In a lean season, officials open the royal granaries that Cleomenes had filled and issue measured rations in your district. Clerks write each household's name against its share.

influences.label: A teacher took you in hand for a season and drilled your letters.
A reader lent you a book roll and talked it over with you.
A veteran took you under his wing and taught you to keep your footing.
A soldier warned you that the recruiters were coming, so you put food and silver aside.
A merchant extended you credit on easy terms when you needed it.
A trader hired you for a season of paid work at the quays.
A workshop master took you on and taught you the trade's first skills.
A craftsman shared part of a paid commission with you.
An interpreter of the sky read a favourable omen for you.
A sky-watcher warned of a hard year, and your household stored food against it.
A musician's playing lifted your spirits through a hard week.
A troupe of performers lent your household a hand when it was struggling.
